summary: EarthSleuth turns 24 years of NASA data (2001–2024) into honest answers about how the Mediterranean and North Africa are changing. For air temperature, rainfall, soil moisture, evapotranspiration and vegetation, it shows what changed, where, by how much, and whether the change is statistically real or could be chance, across 743 places on a 1° grid and 8 sub-regions. Anyone can click a place, type a city or ask a question in plain English. An AI investigator runs the tests and writes the answer, and every number in it is checked against the computed results. When the data can't tell, the site says so.
details:
What exactly does it do?

EarthSleuth is a website that tells you whether the environment around the Mediterranean and North Africa is really changing, or whether you're just looking at noise. It uses 24 years of NASA data (2001–2024) for five variables: air temperature, rainfall, soil moisture, evapotranspiration and vegetation. For each one it shows what changed, where, by how much, and whether the change is statistically significant, across 743 places on a 1° grid and 8 sub-regions. You can click any place, type a city, or ask a question in plain English and get a checked answer.

How does it work?

1. Data: monthly NASA datasets (MERRA-2, GPM IMERG, GLDAS Noah, Terra MODIS) are downloaded with NASA Earthdata and averaged onto a 1° land grid.

2. Statistics, in plain code: we remove the seasonal cycle, measure the trend with a Theil–Sen slope and its 95% range, test it with Mann–Kendall (Hamed–Rao correction for autocorrelation), and control false alarms across the map with Benjamini–Hochberg at 10%. When a trend is too weak to call, we estimate how many years of data it would take.

3. Knowledge graph: datasets, variables, scientific papers and our findings are linked in a graph, checked against NASA CMR and Crossref.

4. AI investigator, in 7 steps: it understands the question, plans which variables to test, runs the statistics, records the findings, looks for published explanations, checks itself and explains. Gemini only reads and writes. Every number in the answer must match the computed results, and each claim is labelled observed, literature or hypothesis.

5. Website, in five steps: Discover, Explore, Investigate, Understand, Conclude. The last one is a downloadable report with every source.

What benefits does it have?

It teaches the difference between a trend and noise on real data, and it says so when the data can't tell. Every number can be traced to a NASA dataset and a test. It's also useful locally: since 2001, Tunisia has warmed by 0.41 °C per decade, lost 1.89 mm/month of rainfall per decade, and its soils are drying, and all three pass the test.

What do you hope to achieve?

We want students, teachers, journalists and curious people to be able to check climate claims themselves instead of trusting a chart. Next steps: comparing two regions in one question, more regions and variables, a classroom game ("Signal or noise?"), and opening the engine so other apps can use it.

What tools did you use?

Python (FastAPI, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, xarray, statsmodels, pyMannKendall, scikit-learn, earthaccess), TypeScript and React (Vite, Tailwind CSS, MapLibre, Recharts), Neo4j for the knowledge graph, and the Google Gen AI SDK (Gemini). It runs in Docker on Render, built from GitHub (https://github.com/b-draoui/earthsleuth). No special hardware, just our laptops.
